title: The Moleka Grid: Toward an Ontological Refoundation of Innovation Studies
content: Innovation studies have experienced remarkable theoretical expansion over the past century. From Schumpeterian economics to innovation systems, socio-technical transitions, complexity theory, and responsible innovation, the field has progressively widened its analytical scope. Yet despite this diversification, a common limitation persists: innovation remains predominantly analyzed through observable outputs, institutional arrangements, and dynamic interactions, while the deeper assumptions that constitute the very conditions of innovation remain largely unexplored. This article argues that innovation studies face a foundational problem rather than a merely empirical one. Existing frameworks provide increasingly sophisticated accounts of how innovation occurs, but offer limited insight into why particular forms of innovation emerge, become legitimate, stabilize, or fail across different contexts. The paper contends that this limitation reflects the absence of an explicit ontological dimension within the dominant architecture of innovation theory. To address this gap, the article introduces the Moleka Grid as a meta-theoretical framework designed to reorganize innovation analysis around three interconnected layers: the symptomatic layer, encompassing observable outputs and measurable effects; the paradigmatic layer, comprising institutional logics, cognitive frameworks, and socio-technical structures; and the ontological layer, referring to foundational assumptions about reality, value, agency, and the nature of change. Unlike existing approaches, the Moleka Grid does not seek to explain specific innovation processes. Rather, it provides an analytical architecture capable of locating and integrating competing theories within a common conceptual space. In this sense, the framework functions as a theory of theories, enabling scholars to examine how different innovation paradigms rest upon implicit ontological commitments. The article develops four central propositions. First, innovation is not merely the production of novelty but the reconfiguration of meaning structures that make novelty possible. Second, all innovation systems are underpinned by ontological assumptions that shape what counts as knowledge, value, and legitimate transformation. Third, innovation trajectories are conditioned by the degree of coherence between ontological, paradigmatic, and symptomatic dimensions. Fourth, major transformations occur when ontological assumptions themselves become objects of innovation. The contribution is therefore not a new model of innovation, but a reframing of innovation studies as an ontologically grounded field of inquiry. By making explicit what has traditionally remained implicit, the Moleka Grid advances an ontological turn in innovation research and provides a foundation for future work on transformative change, epistemic pluralism, sustainability transitions, and postcolonial innovation futures.
